title: Opioids: safe prescribing, conversions, and tapering

source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-09-13. Based on the 2022 CDC clinical practice guideline for prescribing opioids. Not tied to an article; review before trusting.

questions.q: For acute musculoskeletal pain, what is tried before an opioid?
questions.a: Non-opioid analgesics such as NSAIDs and acetaminophen, with non-drug measures
questions.why: For most acute pain the non-opioid options are as effective. If an opioid is needed it is immediate release, at the lowest dose, for three to seven days.

questions.q: When an opioid is needed for acute pain, what supply is usually enough?
questions.why: Longer initial prescriptions predict long-term use. Extended-release or long-acting opioids are not started for acute pain.

questions.q: Above what daily morphine milligram equivalent does the guideline advise particular caution and reassessment?
questions.why: The 2022 guideline removed hard ceilings but kept 50 as the point where overdose risk rises steeply and benefit rarely keeps pace. Above 90 needs a specific justification.

questions.q: Which situations call for co-prescribing naloxone?
a: A history of overdose or substance use disorder
d: A single dose after a dental procedure
questions.why: The patient and the household are taught to use it. Many jurisdictions now recommend it with any opioid prescription, which is a reasonable default.

questions.q: Which combination carries the highest risk of fatal respiratory depression?
d: An opioid with gabapentin at a low dose
questions.why: Gabapentinoids add risk too, especially with kidney impairment. Alcohol counts as a sedative in this calculation.

questions.q: Before prescribing a controlled substance, which database is checked?
questions.a: The state prescription drug monitoring programme
questions.why: It is rechecked at least every three months during ongoing therapy, along with urine drug testing at the start and at least annually.

questions.q: What is the morphine milligram equivalent conversion factor for oxycodone?
questions.why: So 20 mg of oxycodone a day is 30 MME. Hydrocodone is 1, codeine 0.15, tramadol 0.2, and methadone rises with dose and needs a table.

questions.q: When rotating from one opioid to another, by how much is the calculated equivalent dose reduced for incomplete cross-tolerance?
questions.why: The new drug is often more potent than the tables predict. The reduced dose is then titrated up against pain over days.

questions.q: For a patient on long-term opioids, what is a usual tapering rate?
questions.a: About 10% of the dose per month
options: About 10% of the dose per month
questions.why: Faster tapers, 10% a week, suit short-term use. Abrupt discontinuation causes withdrawal, uncontrolled pain, and has been linked to suicide and overdose; the taper is collaborative.

questions.q: Which bowel regimen is started with any regular opioid?
questions.a: A scheduled stimulant laxative such as senna
questions.why: Opioid constipation does not wear off with time and docusate alone does little. Osmotic laxatives are added if the stimulant is not enough.

questions.q: Which opioid is preferred for a patient with kidney failure?
questions.why: Morphine's active metabolites accumulate and cause sedation and myoclonus; codeine and meperidine have the same problem. Methadone is safe in kidney failure but needs an expert.

questions.q: A patient on long-term opioids shows loss of control, craving and continued use despite harm. What is the treatment?
questions.a: Buprenorphine or methadone for opioid use disorder
questions.why: Any prescriber with a DEA registration can now prescribe buprenorphine. Continuing the taper alone in a patient with a use disorder raises the risk of overdose.
